articles.body:
'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

Amid a legal ban on publishing new opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.

However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

Spain’s election: the end of a leftwing icon? - podcast

He has become an icon of the European left. A great political survivor, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez has been in power for eight years while – across the continent – the right has been on the march.

The Socialist party leader has championed immigration, stood up to Donald Trump and been a notable voice for Palestinians in Gaza.

But on Sunday, Sánchez might be replaced by a conservative government in league with the far right.

Madrid correspondent Sam Jones and European community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam report on a pivotal Spanish election, and the gamble that led Sánchez to call it.

Where will this leave the left in Spain, asks Nosheen Iqbal, and across Europe too?

Norse Atlantic budget carrier files for bankruptcy

In other news, budget carrier Norse Atlantic said on Friday it would file a petition for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit, becoming the latest airline to succumb to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war in Iran.

“Norse Atlantic has stopped flying. All flights operated by Norse Atlantic Airways AS and Norse Atlantic UK Ltd from 27 November at 14.00 CET are cancelled. This includes return flights. Please do not go to the airport for a cancelled flight,” the company said in a statement on its website.

The airline failed to pay its employees’ November salaries this week, a pilot union said Thursday, as reported by AFP.

Norse is the second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings this year after Latvia’s airBaltic, highlighting the toll of the Iran war on carriers that entered the crisis without fuel hedges as jet fuel prices surged, Reuters noted.

The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding to file a bankruptcy petition on 27 November with the Agder District Court in Norway for its operating subsidiary.

Will Spain’s housing crisis bring the far right to power? – video

As mass protests over a nationwide housing crisis have forced Sánchez into an early general election, the Guardian travelled to Spain’s Andalusian coast to find out what’s driving the housing crisis, what solutions are on offer and why rightwing populists are gaining ground.

In Spain, the parties are set to hold their closing rallies this evening, with the Socialists and the Broad Front choosing Madrid for their events.

Meanwhile, the PP and Vox have opted for Seville and Valencia.

Spaniards observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power

Eoghan Gilmartin

Freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast

Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past.

Yet since its disappointing showing at the 2023 general election, Abascal has purged much of the party’s original leadership and overseen an ideological renewal.

In looking to update its messaging, Vox has blended elements of Marine Le Pen’s welfare chauvinism, such as the concept of “national priority”, with ideas coming from the pan-European, white nationalist identitarian movement.

Virtually absent from Spanish political debate a year ago, national priority would give Spaniards preferential access to social housing, public services and welfare benefits, with Vox already securing PP backing for the principle in regional coalition deals.

In September, however, the European Commission warned that even the residence-based criteria used at a regional level could discriminate against citizens of other EU member states. Vox’s general election manifesto goes further, pledging to exclude all non-Spanish citizens from the country’s minimum-income benefit.

If the polls are right, PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo could become prime minister on a lower vote share than the PP secured in the last election. He would then owe his majority to Vox’s surge and support in coalition, and Abascal would have both the leverage and the incentive to show his voters what the party can deliver in office.

A coalition formed on those terms could also foreshadow a closer alliance between conservatives and the far right at a European level. A Le Pen victory in the French presidential election next spring would put the nationalist right at the head of one of the EU’s two most influential states, shifting the political centre of gravity in Brussels and opening the way for a durable governing bloc to the right of the EU’s traditional grand coalition.

It was not by chance that Vox opened its election campaign with a rally displaying video messages of support from Le Pen, Meloni and AfD’s Alice Weidel. Having drawn on its far-right European allies to reinvent itself, Vox could now in turn strengthen their hand if it is successful in becoming the PP’s kingmaker after Sunday’s vote.

Sánchez’s defeat would also deprive the centre left of its strongest counterweight in the European Council, where he is the only social democrat to represent one of the EU’s major powers.

Speaking to the Vox rally, Weidel proclaimed: “All of Europe is waiting for a political change in Madrid.” All of Europe may not be waiting for such a change, but it is certainly watching.

Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more

Ashifa Kassam

European community affairs correspondent

Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said.

“But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”

On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.

No new polls are allowed to be published in Spain in the five days before a Spanish election, but one company has found a surprising solución alternativa.

The Adelaide Review ran from 1984 to 2020, covering the city’s cultural and artistic life until Covid and upheavals in the media world made it “untenable”, its editor, Amanda Pepe, wrote in the final edition.

But now it has found unexpected new life as an, erm, back passage for Spanish polls in the blackout period.

The Review site is now owned by a company called Prensa Ibérica, which also runs the Spanish newspaper El Periódico.

An article on the Periódico website that links to the poll criticises “outdated legislation” that lets political parties see polls, but not citizens.

“The Adelaide Review’s daily poll addresses this issue, giving citizens access to the same information used by politicians,” it said.

Join us Sunday night for live blog on 2026 Spanish election

Jakub Krupa

It’s probably a good moment to say that we will be running a special Europe live blog from Madrid on Sunday night to bring you all the latest in the Spanish parliamentary election, including first polls, projections, reactions, and analysis.

Make sure to tune in on Sunday late afternoon and evening.

'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

Amid a legal ban on publishing new opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.

However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

Spain’s ‘rambling’ closing debate sparks row over opposition leader’s ‘sexist’ remark

Sam Jones

in Madrid

Last night’s debate between the leaders of Spain’s four biggest political parties was a rambling, ratty and revealing spectacle in which Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, is generally agreed to have come out on top.

Colau, a former Barcelona mayor, was committed and forensic in her attacks on Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, over his refusal to condemn gender-based violence.

She and the socialist leader and current prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, also joined forces to question the economic wisdom of the far-right party’s plans for €112bn of public spending costs, and to defend the benefits of immigration.

Sánchez – who was far more animated and engaged in this debate than in last week’s head-to-head with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP) – was happy to wind up his rival over his lack of English skills.

Before Feijóo could answer a question from Colau about the PP’s proposed tax cuts, Sánchez – a fluent English speaker – quipped:

“I’m sorry to say that Mr Feijóo’s maths are about as good as his English.”

Vox’s Abascal was keen to keep the focus on immigration and on corruption – a problem, he added, “that ruins and kills”.

He argued that his 30-year political career was unblemished by corruption allegations while suggesting that Sánchez was a “corruption magnet”. That led the prime minister to bring up the infamous mid-1990s holiday photos that show Feijóo hanging out on a boat with his friend Marcial Dorado, who was later convicted of drug trafficking.

But the biggest moment of the night came when Colau asked Feijóo how he could claim to be a good leader when his party had doggedly stood by Carlos Mazón, the PP president of the Valencia region who was eventually forced to resign over his disastrous handling of the floods two years ago that killed more than 230 people.

“Look, good management is taking charge in a national emergency and not running away from Paiporta,” Feijóo said in reference to Sánchez’s hasty exit from one of the areas that was worst hit by the floods after angry locals pelted him with mud during a visit shortly after the disaster.

But it was what came next that caused a stir. Turning to Colau – who, by the time of the floods in the autumn of 2024, had left the Barcelona mayoralty and no longer held public office – Feijóo said, “Y usted calladita” which translates as, “And there wasn’t a peep out of you”.

He accompanied those words putting his finger to his lips – a gesture some took to be a sexist shushing of the Broad Front leader.

Although Feijóo seemed to be trying to claim that Colau had remained silent over the floods when they happened, some took his words as an attempt to tell her to be quiet.

Sánchez was quick to pounce. “Why are you saying, ‘Not a peep out of you’, Mr Feijóo?” the prime minister asked the PP leader. “What kind of sexism is that, Mr Feijóo,” Sánchez added.

Feijóo accused Sánchez of trying to twist his words, but the damage was done. Speaking after the debate, the PP leader issued a semi-apology.

“If I’ve offended anyone, I of course take it back,” he said, adding that he hadn’t been telling Colau to be quiet. But he couldn’t resist arguing that Sánchez leftwing allies had kept quiet “during all the years of corruption”.

Colau herself said the PP leader’s words undermined his supposed feminist credentials. Speaking after the debate, she said:

“I think it was very clear what [Feijóo] was trying to do when he said ‘calladita’. That clearly sexist behaviour was witnessed on TV by all of Spain … As women we will not stop and we will not shut up. No one will make us shut up and we will go and vote.”

And since Spain’s Pedro Sánchez skipped the summit altogether as he’s dramatically fighting for his future ahead of this Sunday’s parliamentary election…

… let’s cross to Madrid for an update on last night’s TV debate…

EU budget talks break down, set to resume in mid-December

In yesterday’s blog, I promised to give you an update this morning on the EU summit, which continued into the small hours.

Well, not much happened, as the talks on the bloc’s next budget collapsed with no agreement, with a group of countries reportedly refusing to take part in further pointless meetings.

The format set the “Sensible Seven” of frugal countries against “Friends of Cohesion” calling for sustained EU spending. With a bit of theatre, everyone disagreed with everyone, and the talks broke down shortly after midnight.

Hungary’s PM Péter Magyar said the discussions would resume at the next summit in December, but warned “there seems to be little chance of reaching a compromise on the EU’s seven-year budget.”

But Germany’s Friedrich Merz tried to stay upbeat:

“Views on the EU budget still differ widely. What is needed now is realism and goodwill. I am confident that we can reach an agreement this year – for a strong economy and a secure Europe.”

There is a bit of urgency there, as France’s Emmanuel Macron wants the discussion on the bloc’s new €1.78tn budget for 2028-2034 to be agreed before the end of the year, and well clear of the French parliamentary elections next spring.

Nato jets scrambled after drone 'briefly' enters Latvian airspace from Russia

Overnight, Nato fighter jets and an interceptor drone were scrambled overnight in Latvia after a drone briefly entered the country’s airspace near its border with Russia, the army said.

Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.

This year, two drones were shot down over Latvia by Nato fighter jets, which protect the skies of Baltic states, Reuters reported.

An army statement said that during the night from Thursday to Friday a drone “briefly flew over Latvian territory” near the border with Russia.

“Fighter jets from Nato’s air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed,” it said, without specifying the origin of the drone.

Morning opening: Putin 'cannot be a friend,' Zelenskyy says on Trump's comments

Jakub Krupa

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US president Donald Trump comment’s hailing Russia’s Vladimir Putin as a friend is “the same that somebody’d say about Hitler during the second world war that he’s a good friend.”

Talking to BBC in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Trump’s comments were “strange,” adding:

“He’s an aggressor … and a killer. He cannot be a friend. Just cannot be.”

In a pointed criticism of the US position, he said:

“We need American position to be American. We don’t need signals – I mean from the US – which we can get from Russia.”

Urging the US to use its “power and respect” to push Moscow more, he said:

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right.”

His latest comments come as Russian attacks on Ukraine continue, amid growing concern over the upcoming winter as the strikes repeatedly hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

I will bring you more on this throughout the day.

I will also update you on last night’s EU summit, the final TV debate in Spain ahead of Sunday’s elections, and many more.

It’s Friday, 27 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.body:
Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy amid rising fuel costs

November 27, 2026

The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

articles.title: Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
articles.summary: Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
articles.preview: Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security. articles.body:
Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.

Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.

Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.

Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.

Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.

“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here,” Badilla continued without elaborating. “Our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system.”

While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.

On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.

Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the university has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.

Why would Israel celebrate a UN figure not being allowed entry to Costa Rica?

As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide, for which she received numerous threats, Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.

Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.

She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.

In her July 2025 report, she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google, alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.

On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”

Who is Francesca Albanese?

Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.

After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.

Is this the first time Israel and its allies have targeted Albanese?

No.

Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.

The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.

In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.

The most significant escalation came in July 2025, when the Trump administration imposed sanctions against Albanese, accusing her of pursuing a campaign of political and economic warfare against Israel and the United States.

The measures included restrictions on Albanese entering the US, blocking her property and financial interests subject to US jurisdiction and prohibiting US nationals from engaging in transactions with her, effectively isolating her from much of the US financial system.

The US decision was roundly condemned by the UN and various rights groups.

A committee of the UN’s Human Rights Council characterised it as just one aspect of the “continued assault of the current US administration on the entire UN system and its core values of human rights, justice, accountability and the rule of law”. Rights groups, including Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International, also criticised the decision, with the latter slamming the US measures as a “disgraceful affront to international justice”.

articles.title: US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live
articles.summary: US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 11:20 'Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,' says advert, over backdrop of amputee child in Gaza A screengrab from the advert (No More For Israel) Off A 30-second advert highlighting US taxpayer funding for Israel was broadcast across the United States on Wednesday night during a Thanksgiving special edition of the long-running sketch show Saturday Night Live. The ad, from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project (Imeu), a pro- Palestinian advocacy group based in California, shows an American girl carrying out chores over the course of the year in order to make $400 to buy a new bicycle. The footage then cuts from the American on a pristine suburban street to a Palestinian girl amid the rubble of Gaza. The Palestinian girl has lost a leg to Israeli bombs and is on crutches. “Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,” says the ad's American narrator, against the backdrop of the girl in Gaza. The US currently officially gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds. The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes, meaning that the advert's figure is accurate. At the end of the ad, the viewer is directed to a website called No More For Israel , which tells you that "the US government has sent Israel over $330bn in inflation-adjusted dollars since 1948. That’s $400 every three seconds non-stop for nearly 80 years." "Right now, behind closed doors, the White House is negotiating a new long-term weapons giveaway to Israel that is estimated to send at least $19bn more of our tax dollars to Israel over the next five years: another $400 every three seconds," the site says. 'Antisemitic Hamas propaganda' Israeli newspapers, the country's foreign ministry and pro-Israel figures in the US have hit out at broadcaster NBC for airing the advert. End Jew Hatred, a group linked to the Lawfare Project, called the advert "antisemitic Hamas propaganda" and circulated a petition demanding that NBC stop broadcasting it. Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book rote on X : "Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible. "Again and again, why do people in positions of authority fail to demonstrate basic decency, let alone respect, for the Jewish community? At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative." Greenblatt did not elaborate on what the "twisted narrative" of the advert was or offer any evidence for why its claims were "false". Self-described "accidental activist" Samantha Ettus said that the advert "promotes the lie that Israel deliberately targets children", more than 22,000 of whom have been killed in Gaza by Israel. "It never mentions Hamas. It never mentions October 7, the hostages, or the rockets Israel is defending against," Ettus posted on X . Israel’s foreign ministry said: “Don’t let anyone exploit your loved ones’ compassion this holiday season. Ask who’s funding this campaign, whose real goal is the destruction of Israel.” “We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,” Margaret DeReus, Imeu's executive director, told Semafor. Viewing figures for Wednesday's broadcast have yet to be released, but last year's Thanksgiving special attracted approximately 2.7 million viewers. articles.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties. Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.

"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

articles.body:
El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.

Hunger is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme climate events, two United Nations agencies said in a new report.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats of famine, driven by violence, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather, including the El Nino phenomenon.

Listings in the report, released twice a year through the Global Network Against Food Crises, have risen from 13 hotspots in June, with Chad, Uganda and parts of both Southern Africa and Central America added, while Lebanon was removed.

Armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, the report said, as soaring food, energy and transport costs were eroding people’s ability to feed themselves.

El Nino, which is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots: Southern Africa, the Central American Dry Corridor and northeastern Uganda.

Covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was affecting efforts to avert catastrophe.

In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1bn to $2bn.

“While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote the FAO and WFP.

While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks – including risk of famine – re-emerged within a few years.”

In Sudan, famine remains a risk in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, as fighting disrupts food production, markets and aid deliveries.

The agencies also identified famine risks in parts of Somalia and South Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation.

Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Gaza were also classified as areas of very great concern.

Gaza was downgraded from the highest level of concern after small improvements in food security following the October 2025 “ceasefire”. But agencies warned that conditions remained fragile in Gaza, while in the occupied West Bank, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen.

articles.title: Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator?
articles.summary: Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator? Submitted by Peter Oborne on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 15:53 These cross-bench jollification ceremonies might appear innocent at a glance - until you dig deeper into the magazine's coverage of Islam Andy Burnham speaks after being confirmed as the Labour Party’s new leader and Britain’s next prime minister, during a conference in central London on 17 July 2026 (AFP) Off The International Court of Justice (ICJ) finally ruled last week that the Myanmar government carried out a genocide when its army slaughtered thousands of Rohingya Muslims in an orgy of planned killing and mass rape. This is the second time that the ICJ has found that genocide was committed against a Muslim population. Twenty years ago, it reached that verdict in the wake of the systematic execution of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. That could become three times if the ICJ ultimately resolves that Israel ’s ongoing slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza - where more than 74,000 have been confirmed dead so far, almost all of them Muslim - amounts to a genocide . The world has become an intolerably dangerous place if you are Muslim. French writer Renaud Camus once warned that Muslim immigration would wipe out white Europeans. “The great replacement is very simple,” he said in 2012 . “You have one people, and in the space of a generation you have a different people.” Meanwhile, China has held hundreds of thousands of Muslims in secretive detention camps in recent years, while the Muslim community in India has been denounced as a “virus” by the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh. This view that Islam is a danger to humanity is impossible to substantiate. When Muslims travel to other countries, they normally arrive as victims of oppression, war or civil conflict, not as aggressors. Yet across much of the globe, Muslims are portrayed as the enemy - and that includes in Britain . Islamophobic tropes Pick up a newspaper. Read a book on current affairs. Consult a think tank. Listen to a politician. Go down to the pub. You will hear the same story: Islam is on the march, hell-bent on destroying the West. Muslims are presented as invaders, enemies of civilisation, parasites, unpatriotic - uncomfortably similar to the tropes deployed before the Srebrenica and Myanmar genocides. According to the British Muslim Trust, there were 78 verified attacks involving mosques over the 12 months to July 2026. In recent decades, several Muslims have been murdered simply for being Muslim , while others get abused, targeted or beaten up. They fear going out at night. This past April, a man was jailed for 13 years after raping a Sikh woman because he believed she was Muslim. It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others failed to show Yet the systematic demonisation of Muslims has become a central part of the narrative of the British political and media classes in the 21st century. As I set out in my book The Fate of Abraham , this rhetoric has strong historical roots. But it is now so much a part of normal discussion that almost nobody notices. At Westminster in particular, there is an adamantine reluctance to challenge the demonisation of a relatively small section of the British population. Politicians are rightly wide awake to the problem of antisemitism , a poisonous virus that has been deeply embedded in western Christian DNA for a millennium of British history. But the majority of British MPs and newspapers flatly refuse to acknowledge that Islamophobia has become a problem in contemporary Britain. Wednesday night provided a powerful and very telling example. Politicians from the main political parties gathered in central London to celebrate the Spectator Parliamentarian of the Year awards . The most senior politicians in Britain were singled out for awards, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch. Former foreign secretary David Lammy and Michael Gove, the former Tory cabinet minister who now edits the Spectator, presented the awards. On the face of things, this was an admirable cross-party event, when journalists and politicians resolved for an evening to overcome their differences and celebrate the fact that we British have the good fortune to live in a parliamentary democracy. (The revered Spectator political columnist Henry Fairlie once memorably recorded that he slept more soundly in his bed when Parliament was sitting). Troubling message But let’s pause a moment and reflect on how all this good cheer and cross-bench jollification looks and feels if you are a British Muslim. This past summer, the Centre for Media Monitoring produced a report on the Spectator’s coverage of Islam. It found that the magazine’s extensive (one might even say obsessive) output on Islam portrays Muslims as invaders who don’t belong in this country, don’t share British values, and threaten our public spaces. The report also documents how Spectator writers substantiate this thesis through misrepresentations, fabrications, vulgar abuse, and conspiracy theories. Some of the examples are horrifying. Many observers would regard such coverage as Islamophobic. Not the Spectator, which refuses to frame Islamophobia in its accepted sense as an irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at Muslims for being Muslim. How mainstream media fuels the UK's Islamophobia crisis he term is a cynical attempt to exempt Muslims from criticism, and to import a blasphemy law through the back door. The magazine ran the headline: “There’s not enough Islamophobia in the Conservative Party.” After an outcry the Spectator changed the headline. But one only has to imagine the career-ending consequences - not just for the writer, but also the editor, and indeed the magazine itself - that would (rightly) follow if a Labour magazine asserted “there’s not enough antisemitism in Labour”. Lammy might be interested to learn that the magazine recently ran two articles calling for the rehabilitation of the racist 20th-century Tory politician Enoch Powell. Defenders of the Spectator are entitled to point out that Britain is a free country, and any magazine or newspaper is permitted to propagate whatever views it likes, no matter how bigoted or divisive, so long as they stay within the law. But that is not the case with political parties. When senior politicians accept awards, they do not send out a message that they agree with the organisers’ beliefs and objectives, and it would be absurd to claim that they do. Yet they are signalling that they regard the Spectator’s commentary on Muslims as within the boundaries of acceptable discourse. It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others, like Zack Polanski’s Green Party, failed to show. When Burnham accepted his well-deserved award as politician of the year (last year’s recipient was Reform UK leader Nigel Farage), he was not endorsing the Spectator’s compulsive hostility to Muslims. But he certainly was sending the message that the Spectator operates within the acceptable boundaries of public discourse when it demonises Muslims. That is a troubling message to send out at any time - all the more so as Islamophobia Awareness Month reaches its climax. Submitted by Peter Oborne on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 15:53 These cross-bench jollification ceremonies might appear innocent at a glance - until you dig deeper into the magazine's coverage of Islam Andy Burnham speaks after being confirmed as the Labour Party’s new leader and Britain’s next prime minister, during a conference in central London on 17 July 2026 (AFP) Off The International Court of Justice (ICJ) finally ruled last week that the Myanmar government carried out a genocide when its army slaughtered thousands of Rohingya Muslims in an orgy of planned killing and mass rape.

This is the second time that the ICJ has found that genocide was committed against a Muslim population. Twenty years ago, it reached that verdict in the wake of the systematic execution of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. That could become three times if the ICJ ultimately resolves that Israel ’s ongoing slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza - where more than 74,000 have been confirmed dead so far, almost all of them Muslim - amounts to a genocide .

The world has become an intolerably dangerous place if you are Muslim. French writer Renaud Camus once warned that Muslim immigration would wipe out white Europeans. “The great replacement is very simple,” he said in 2012 . “You have one people, and in the space of a generation you have a different people.” Meanwhile, China has held hundreds of thousands of Muslims in secretive detention camps in recent years, while the Muslim community in India has been denounced as a “virus” by the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh.

This view that Islam is a danger to humanity is impossible to substantiate. When Muslims travel to other countries, they normally arrive as victims of oppression, war or civil conflict, not as aggressors. Yet across much of the globe, Muslims are portrayed as the enemy - and that includes in Britain . Islamophobic tropes Pick up a newspaper. Read a book on current affairs. Consult a think tank. Listen to a politician.

Go down to the pub. You will hear the same story: Islam is on the march, hell-bent on destroying the West. Muslims are presented as invaders, enemies of civilisation, parasites, unpatriotic - uncomfortably similar to the tropes deployed before the Srebrenica and Myanmar genocides. According to the British Muslim Trust, there were 78 verified attacks involving mosques over the 12 months to July 2026.

In recent decades, several Muslims have been murdered simply for being Muslim , while others get abused, targeted or beaten up. They fear going out at night. This past April, a man was jailed for 13 years after raping a Sikh woman because he believed she was Muslim. It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others failed to show Yet the systematic demonisation of Muslims has become a central part of the narrative of the British political and media classes in the 21st century.

As I set out in my book The Fate of Abraham , this rhetoric has strong historical roots. But it is now so much a part of normal discussion that almost nobody notices. At Westminster in particular, there is an adamantine reluctance to challenge the demonisation of a relatively small section of the British population. Politicians are rightly wide awake to the problem of antisemitism , a poisonous virus that has been deeply embedded in western Christian DNA for a millennium of British history.

But the majority of British MPs and newspapers flatly refuse to acknowledge that Islamophobia has become a problem in contemporary Britain. Wednesday night provided a powerful and very telling example. Politicians from the main political parties gathered in central London to celebrate the Spectator Parliamentarian of the Year awards . The most senior politicians in Britain were singled out for awards, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch.

Former foreign secretary David Lammy and Michael Gove, the former Tory cabinet minister who now edits the Spectator, presented the awards. On the face of things, this was an admirable cross-party event, when journalists and politicians resolved for an evening to overcome their differences and celebrate the fact that we British have the good fortune to live in a parliamentary democracy. (The revered Spectator political columnist Henry Fairlie once memorably recorded that he slept more soundly in his bed when Parliament was sitting).

Troubling message But let’s pause a moment and reflect on how all this good cheer and cross-bench jollification looks and feels if you are a British Muslim. This past summer, the Centre for Media Monitoring produced a report on the Spectator’s coverage of Islam. It found that the magazine’s extensive (one might even say obsessive) output on Islam portrays Muslims as invaders who don’t belong in this country, don’t share British values, and threaten our public spaces.

The report also documents how Spectator writers substantiate this thesis through misrepresentations, fabrications, vulgar abuse, and conspiracy theories. Some of the examples are horrifying. Many observers would regard such coverage as Islamophobic. Not the Spectator, which refuses to frame Islamophobia in its accepted sense as an irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at Muslims for being Muslim.

How mainstream media fuels the UK's Islamophobia crisis he term is a cynical attempt to exempt Muslims from criticism, and to import a blasphemy law through the back door. The magazine ran the headline: “There’s not enough Islamophobia in the Conservative Party.” After an outcry the Spectator changed the headline. But one only has to imagine the career-ending consequences - not just for the writer, but also the editor, and indeed the magazine itself - that would (rightly) follow if a Labour magazine asserted “there’s not enough antisemitism in Labour”.

Lammy might be interested to learn that the magazine recently ran two articles calling for the rehabilitation of the racist 20th-century Tory politician Enoch Powell. Defenders of the Spectator are entitled to point out that Britain is a free country, and any magazine or newspaper is permitted to propagate whatever views it likes, no matter how bigoted or divisive, so long as they stay within the law.

But that is not the case with political parties. When senior politicians accept awards, they do not send out a message that they agree with the organisers’ beliefs and objectives, and it would be absurd to claim that they do. Yet they are signalling that they regard the Spectator’s commentary on Muslims as within the boundaries of acceptable discourse. It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others, like Zack Polanski’s Green Party, failed to show.

When Burnham accepted his well-deserved award as politician of the year (last year’s recipient was Reform UK leader Nigel Farage), he was not endorsing the Spectator’s compulsive hostility to Muslims. But he certainly was sending the message that the Spectator operates within the acceptable boundaries of public discourse when it demonises Muslims. That is a troubling message to send out at any time - all the more so as Islamophobia Awareness Month reaches its climax.

articles.title: Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
articles.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn. For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
