The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn.

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly last year.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the conflict's impact.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband.

Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRA), said she had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 in year measured roughly from March 2025 to March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson told DW that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs, and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her towards marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

The concerns also extend to the online space. An HRA investigation published in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted or whether the war increased them.

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he told DW. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

articles.title: Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
articles.summary: Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.
articles.preview: Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis. Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group. The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz. The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.

Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group.

The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz.

The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

A local source said that a residential building was struck and that “most” of the victims were children, according to the media report.

Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, the report said. Three people remain missing beneath the rubble.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting the internationally-recognised Yemen government did not immediately comment.

The coalition said later on Friday that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region.

Humanitarian crisis

Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.

Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, as the United States’ war on Iran escalated hostilities and the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.

Some 13,343 people have been killed or injured since August, according to the World Health Organization, while the country is sliding into a humanitarian crisis.

The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme said on Friday that Yemen is among conflict hotspots that face severe food insecurity.

The Norwegian Refugee Council warned this week that the renewed fighting has displaced thousands and piled pressure onto dangerously underfunded aid efforts.

Aid from the US, Germany and others has shrunk considerably in recent years, the nongovernmental organisation noted, saying it has received only 12 percent of funding for emergency shelter support in Yemen so far this year.

“Fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices,” NRC Secretary-General Jan Egeland said, warning that families across Yemen are being pushed deeper into need.

“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here,” Egeland stated.

Calling for better humanitarian access and civilian protection, he demanded that “the powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality”.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
articles.preview: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin. "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

- Published7 days ago

- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published6 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: Algeria condemns 'spillover' of Ukraine war into Libya
articles.summary: Algeria on Thursday condemned what it called the ‘spillover’ of the war in Ukraine into Libya, after Kyiv’s attack on two Russian vessels off eastern Libya. Two Libyan soldiers were killed in Sunday’s drone strikes which sank a Russian warship and targeted a cargo ship in Libyan waters.
articles.preview: Algeria on Thursday condemned what it called the ‘spillover’ of the war in Ukraine into Libya, after Kyiv’s attack on two Russian vessels off eastern Libya. Two Libyan soldiers were killed in Sunday’s drone strikes which sank a Russian warship and targeted a cargo ship in Libyan waters.
articles.body:
Libya

Algeria on Thursday said it opposed the "spillover" of the Ukraine war in Libya after Kyiv carried out a deadly attack on two Russian ships off the eastern city of Benghazi, calling for an end to its neighbour's political divide.

"We do not accept a spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war in our region," said Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, adding the ship attacks could "only be condemned."

Attaf said Ukraine's drone strikes on Sunday, which killed two Libyan soldiers, also came as "a stark reminder of the urgent need to reach a solution that ends the crisis" in Libya.

"The divide in Libya is deep on all levels," the diplomat said, calling for "an inclusive political process that leads to unified and legitimate institutions... free from foreign dictates."

Libya has been split between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, who has maintained close ties with Russia and the United Arab Emirates.

Attaf said issues in Libya and the Sahel were "interconnected", adding that Algeria's "main source of concern" was foreign interference.

The minister did not name any foreign country interfering in Libya and the Sahel, but Algiers has often accused the UAE of meddling in the region. Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the Gulf country in September after years of tensions.

In an unprecedented move last month, the Algerian parliament also approved deploying Algerian troops to Niger, with the stated aim of "protecting energy installations" near their shared border.

But reports indicated that Algerian troops would be housed in a base in Madama, a desert area closer to southern Libya.

articles.title: A decade after Duterte's drug war, the Philippines confronts its bloody legacy as ICC trial looms
articles.summary: Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.
articles.preview: Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.
articles.body:
Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.

MANILA / THE HAGUE: At De La Salle University in Manila, a brightly painted van stands out on campus.

The words “Stop the killings” are emblazoned across its side. A mural depicts a woman cradling her dead family. Between windows, a huge “X” crosses over a skull and the words “death squad”.

Above the windscreen is a simple message: “Coffee. Stories. Human rights.”

This is no ordinary coffee van.

It is run by Silingan Coffee, a social enterprise that offers employment to families who lost loved ones during former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's bloody war on drugs.

Beyond serving coffee and pastries, the project provides a space for survivors to share their stories, spread awareness about the killings and keep their pursuit of justice alive.

“This is the Justice Van. It's been to a lot of places,” said Grace Garganta, the brand’s operations head.

“What we really hope for with Silingan is not only to sell coffee. We really need justice. We believe that seeking justice means we can't just be silent.”

Founded in 2021 with a single outlet in Quezon City, Silingan has since expanded to six branches across the Greater Manila Area, providing jobs to members of more than 40 families affected by the drug war.

Many of its employees are mothers, widows and daughters of those killed.

“Here at Silingan, we don't look at your educational background. The only thing we look for is a death certificate and a police report. These are proof that you are a victim or a relative of a victim of the war on drugs,” said Garganta.

“When (customers) learn we're all from families of victims of extrajudicial killings, they're surprised. We don't force anyone to listen to us or believe us. What matters is for us to be heard,” the 34-year-old added.

“(Silingan) doesn't just give us job opportunities. It also gives us dignity.”

LIVING WITH THE SCARS OF THE DRUG WAR

For Garganta, the struggle for justice is deeply personal.

Her father and brother were killed just three weeks after Duterte launched his nationwide anti-drug campaign in 2016.

“My father was killed inside our home. My brother was taken from our home and dumped in a grassy field. They said my father resisted arrest,” she told CNA.

“I was a student and had to stop studying. I had to find a job because I had to feed and support my siblings. But instead of being able to earn a living, I had to lie low.”

Fearing that she too could be targeted, Garganta sought refuge at Baclaran Church in 2017.

“I was afraid of staying outside. I think if I hadn't fled to the church, I would probably be dead too. I'm deeply grateful to the people in the church who really supported me,” she said.

Her experience reflects the fear that gripped many communities during Duterte's crackdown.

Families of those killed often faced not only the loss of their loved ones, but also the stigma of being associated with illegal drugs and the fear of further harassment or violence.

Duterte had repeatedly urged law enforcement officers to take a hard line against suspected drug offenders, including using lethal force when confronted with violent resistance.

Human rights groups condemned the campaign as a war against the poor.

Many of those killed were fathers and sons who were breadwinners, leaving wives, mothers and other relatives to support their families.

At another Silingan Coffee branch at the Monument of Heroes in Quezon City, one mother still struggles with the loss of her son.

He had been earning a living as a tricycle driver when he was shot dead by an unidentified assailant on Christmas Day. He was 21 years old.

“I took on all kinds of honest work to provide for my family so we could survive hardship and get through each day, only for my son’s dreams to be shattered,” she said.

“Instead of being able to help support the family, my son was killed. The person just shot him, then ran off. He was hit in the back of his neck. My son died on Dec 25. We held his wake and we were grieving at Christmas.”

The gunfire also killed his passenger, a 16-year-old neighbour.

When Duterte was arrested last year, she felt that justice might finally be within reach.

“We were relieved, as if a weight was lifted from us. We thought at last we will get our due. I hope we win. We really hope that if (Duterte is found guilty), he will stay in prison,” she said.

For years, families have struggled to secure accountability through the Philippine justice system. Despite attempts to prosecute police officers implicated in drug war killings, convictions have been rare.

In March 2025, Philippine authorities arrested Duterte and transferred the 81-year-old to the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, where he faces trial for crimes against humanity.

Garganta, who works at Silingan Coffee’s justice van, also hopes the international proceedings will deliver answers that have long eluded victims.

“I hope he (Duterte) stays safe and healthy because while he is strong and alive, the trial can continue,” she said. “I don't hope for his death. I hope the trial can proceed swiftly, so that families like us can quickly attain justice.”

A COUNTRY CONFRONTS ITS PAST

Duterte swept to power in 2016 on a promise to eradicate illegal drugs and restore law and order.

What followed was a campaign of bloodshed that shocked the country and drew international condemnation.

Night after night, suspected drug offenders were killed in impoverished neighbourhoods, some by police officers claiming self-defence, and others by masked vigilantes on motorcycles.

The Philippine government puts the death toll at around 6,000, but human rights groups estimate that between 12,000 and 30,000 people were killed.

Away from the bustling streets of Metro Manila, La Loma Cemetery offers a quiet refuge from the noise of the surrounding city. There, an unimposing structure called Dambana ng Paghilom, or Shrine of Healing, stands as a reminder of one of the darkest chapters in recent Philippine history.

With 100 vaults that can hold as many as six urns each, the shrine serves as a final resting place for just a fraction of the thousands who lost their lives during Duterte's crackdown.

Catholic priest Flavie Villanueva led the construction of the memorial to offer a place of dignity for the dead and healing for those left behind.

Through his Program Paghilom initiative, he has supported devastated families and helped survivors cope with grief, rebuild their lives and seek justice.

But even after a decade of working with victims, he continues to grapple with how such violence could have unfolded in a deeply religious country.

“Why did a Catholic country with deep faith and devotion go through this bloody nightmare? Where did we go wrong? How can we make right the bad choices we made in the past?” he asked.

In September this year, Duterte made his first physical pre-trial appearance before the ICC.

The court has found “reasonable grounds” to believe that he is individually responsible as an indirect co-perpetrator of killings between November 2011 and March 2019, covering part of his tenure as mayor of Davao City and the first three years of his presidency.

For the families of those killed, the proceedings offer a long-awaited opportunity for accountability.

But former Filipino ICC judge Raul Pangalangan believes a criminal conviction alone would not be enough to address the damage left behind.

“Of course, a finding of guilt in a criminal case is important ... but that alone won’t suffice. We would have to reach out to victim communities to assure them that those years, when everyone looked the other way, will not happen again,” he said.

Pangalangan now chairs a newly formed independent Truth Commission, which aims to establish a credible record of the violence through testimonies and documentary evidence from victims' families, witnesses and even perpetrators.

Its work seeks to address questions that go beyond who ordered or carried out the killings: how did the violence become possible, and why was it accepted – even celebrated – by sections of society?

THE APPEAL OF A STRONGMAN

Sociologist Filomin Gutierrez said the answer lies partly in long-standing public frustration over crime, inequality and economic progress that has failed to benefit many Filipinos.

Duterte tapped into those grievances by presenting himself as a decisive leader willing to use force to restore order.

“The nostalgia for a strong-arm leader was there, and Duterte spoke the language,” said Gutierrez, a University of the Philippines (UP) professor.

“He had charisma and he was able to usher the drug crisis into the picture and convince everyone that if we get rid of the drug problem, then we get rid of the crime problem.”

She warned that the acceptance of violence as a solution to social problems could have consequences far beyond Duterte's presidency – it could normalise the use of strongman tactics by politicians.

“When you have a leader who advocates and relies on violence as a solution to political, social, economic or whatever problem, then it may not only activate the official channels such as the PNP (national police), but will also activate the dormant violent sources within the community – the ones they call vigilantes, the ones they call death squads,” she said.

Despite his detention in The Hague, Duterte and his family remain widely popular and politically influential.

His daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, is widely regarded as a leading contender for the 2028 presidential election.

Political observers say she has drawn heavily on her father's political appeal and style of governance, often described as “Dutertismo”.

But the ICC proceedings could influence the country's political landscape, said UP political science professor Jean Encinas Franco.

“Filipinos have normalised electing people from political dynasties. It's very easy for them to transfer their support for Rodrigo Duterte to Sara Duterte,” she said.

“(But) if Duterte is convicted, then his opponents or Sara Duterte's opponents in the 2028 elections can actually use it to say: ‘Hey, we were right in the first place’.”

Franco believes Duterte's enduring popularity reflects a conviction among many Filipinos that his drug war made the country safer.

“A large part of the public remained supportive of Duterte and allowed him to do what he did because they firmly believed that it was something that will save them from the so-called dregs in their communities,” she said.

ON TRIAL IN THE HAGUE

More than 11,000km away, in the Netherlands, the man at the centre of the case is being held at an ICC detention facility.

Duterte is awaiting proceedings scheduled to begin on Monday (Nov 30).

He faces allegations relating to 85 murders and two attempted murders linked to his anti-drug campaign. His defence team has told judges he denies the charges.

If convicted of any of three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.

The former president's arrest in March 2025 made him the first former Asian leader to be taken into ICC custody.

Since then, court proceedings have become a focal point for both supporters and critics, exposing deep divisions among Filipinos over the former president’s controversial drug war.

Outside the court in The Hague, activists have demanded accountability for those killed, while Duterte's supporters have questioned his transfer to international custody and called for his release.

“It should have been handled first in the Philippines before they sent (the case) here. I feel like they sold the former president here like a piece of meat,” said one supporter.

An activist offered a starkly different perspective.

“We're here reminding people that he's now afforded the right to be faced in court, which a lot of the victims were not able to during the extrajudicial killings and the war on drugs in the Philippines,” she told CNA.

Among those campaigning for accountability are Patricia Enriquez and Fiona Magallanes, who moved from the Philippines to Europe as students.

They are organisers of the Netherlands branch of Duterte Panagutin Europe, a group advocating justice for the killings.

Magallanes said living abroad brings a responsibility to speak up for those who may face greater risks at home.

“I feel a responsibility to use my privilege here, living outside of the Philippines, to continue to speak up,” she said.

“People who speak out – they can be threatened with repression, they can be red-tagged, they can be called all kinds of vitriol and ostracised from their communities. But it’s our responsibility as young Filipinos to continue the fight.”

But Duterte's supporters are equally determined to make their voices heard. Some regularly gather outside the detention facility, hoping their presence will lift his spirits.

“Our continued support and unwavering presence sends a signal directly, not to the judges or detractors, but to the former president himself that the Filipino people will never give up on him,” said Alvin Dave Sarzate, who has been living in the Netherlands for eight years.

“It fuels him and hopefully motivates him to fight through until the very end. Hopefully, one day he will be brought back to the Philippines, where he rightfully belongs.”

A LONG ROAD TO JUSTICE

Inside the courtroom, the case faces substantial legal and logistical challenges.

Questions over Duterte's physical and mental health have surfaced, although independent medical experts have found him fit to stand trial.

The scale of the evidence, covering alleged crimes over eight years, also presents a formidable task for prosecutors and defence lawyers.

Presiding judge Joanna Korner has stressed the need to keep proceedings moving expeditiously.

At a status conference on Oct 13, she questioned the prosecution's proposal to introduce clips from 197 of Duterte's speeches as evidence.

“We’re anxious as far as possible in this case to keep the number of hours to the least possible without making it impossible for you to present your case,” she told the prosecution.

British lawyer Peter Haynes, who took over as Duterte's lead counsel in May, has repeatedly clashed with prosecutors over the volume and organisation of documentary evidence submitted in the case.

“We haven't got the resources to go through 35,000 pages of Rule 77 material to find all the cases in which these things were properly investigated (and) all the cases in which there is no relationship to the war on drugs at all,” he said.

The ICC's acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said distilling years of investigations and vast amounts of evidence into a focused case is no easy task.

“Everyone wants to be heard, particularly the victims. This translates into a huge number of documents, sometimes thousands of terabytes,” he told CNA.

But he said reaching the trial stage marks a significant milestone, particularly for those who have come forward to testify.

“Going to trial is extremely important … this is the climax of a long process of work which people do not necessarily see … of everyone who has participated in the building of a case, particularly those who took the risk to provide evidence. That is the biggest moment for justice,” he said.

The legal battle is expected to be lengthy, with the proceedings continuing to stir strong emotions among Filipinos both at home and abroad.

Panagutin Netherlands’ Enriquez said the uncertainty surrounding the case has made the months since Duterte's arrest an emotional roller coaster.

But she believes the proceedings offer something beyond a possible verdict: an opportunity to confront the attitudes that allowed the killings to happen.

“(We’ve been) fighting off fake news (and) false information that people understood from the extrajudicial killings – that they thought it was ok to kill people because they are criminals but actually it’s not,” she said.

“Even if this trial might take a long (time), it’s also an avenue for us to open conversations with a lot of people, not just Filipinos, that this is a system that was created and it’s something we can fight together.”

For legal observers, the ICC's credibility will rest on its ability to examine the evidence impartially and deliver a judgment grounded in law.

As the trial approaches, the divide between Duterte's supporters and critics remains as pronounced as ever.

For some, the proceedings represent a long-awaited reckoning with a campaign that devastated thousands of families. For others, they are a test of whether a former president they continue to admire will receive a fair hearing.

And for families still carrying the grief from the loss of their loved ones, the hope is that the search for justice will finally bring answers, and help ensure that such violence is never repeated.

articles.title: Italy says not informed about Ukraine drone strike on Russian ships in Libya
articles.summary: Italy has joined the voices expressing concern about Ukraine’s attack on Russia ships in Libyan waters. Rome was not informed of Sunday’s drone strike, the country’s foreign minister told parliament on Thursday, warning that further military action could jeopardise efforts to reunify Libya.
articles.preview: Italy has joined the voices expressing concern about Ukraine’s attack on Russia ships in Libyan waters. Rome was not informed of Sunday’s drone strike, the country’s foreign minister told parliament on Thursday, warning that further military action could jeopardise efforts to reunify Libya.
articles.body:
Libya

Italy was not informed of the Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in Libya, its foreign minister said in parliament on Thursday.

Antonio Tajani briefed lawmakers after a Ukrainian sea-drone strike in the eastern Libyan port city of Benghazi against a Russian warship and a cargo vessel.

Tajani said he voiced Italy’s concern about a conflict expansion in the Mediterranean region during a phone call with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybil on Tuesday.

“Our support for Kyiv has not prevented us from expressing strong concerns for the recent Ukrainian attack in Libya, a country where we have important economic and strategic interests,” Tajani said.

The minster said Italy shares the concern for the increasing Russian military presence in western Libya, “We share the concern for the growing presence of hostile actors, specifically Russia, a destabilising factor in the region, few hundred kilometers away from our coasts,” Tajani said.

"We did not know about Kyiv’s intention to strike in Libyan territorial waters, in a port even, and we did not agree with this decision.

We are convinced that violating Libya’s sovereignty is a mistake and that it does not help Ukraine’s cause,” he said.

Oil-rich Libya, a former Italian colony, has been mired in chaos since a NATO-backed uprising in 2011 became a civil war that toppled longtime leader Moammar Gadhafi, who was later killed.

For much of the past decade, the country has remained divided between two administrations backed by rival foreign powers.

Libya is strategically important for Italy, linked to the north-African country with direct oil and gas undersea pipelines. Italian oil giant ENI also runs several major fields and terminals in the west of the country.

The internationally recognised government in Tripoli has cultivated ties with Ukraine and its Western allies, partly to support its efforts to stay in power, and to deter the flow of people hoping to reach Europe as migrants. It is backed by an array of loosely allied armed groups and militias.

The strike in Benghazi was not the first time Ukraine used Libya to attack Russian vessels.

In March, Ukrainian sea drones struck and badly damaged a Russian-flagged tanker carrying liquefied natural gas near Maltese waters.

Sunday’s attack, however, is a potentially significant escalation in Ukraine’s attacks on Russian interests overseas.

Further military actions could further destabilise Libya and jeopardise the international efforts to bring unity to the country.

“We ask all parties to refrain from further military actions in Libyan territory and its waters,” Tajani declared.

articles.body:
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

But, unhappily for Merz, he cannot rely on the wholehearted support of the German public, either. A new survey released this week showed that, for the first time, Kyiv no longer enjoys majority support among the German population. The study by the Körber Foundation, showed 53% of those questioned were against Germany supporting Ukraine militarily, with only 46% in favour – compared with 59% just a year ago.

Merz, whose disapproval ratings stand at a record 88%, is therefore looking increasingly isolated. This all sends a worrying signal to Kyiv, which has counted on Germany as its biggest backer for some time, since Washington largely withdrew its favour.

The government’s attempts to push the case for Ukraine domestically now, when it is arguably most necessary, are not helped by the fact that German leaders have been reluctant to play up the support Germany has given to Kyiv since 2022 for fear of stoking embers of resentment.

This extends to keeping as quiet as possible about the estimated 1.33 million Ukrainians who have been given refuge in Germany since the full-scale invasion of their country, because of the strong tendency of the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland to portray them as a burden.

As the cost of living crisis bites and the German public feels increasingly poorer economically, the debate over Ukraine funding is being framed – misleadingly, say critics – as a contest between the nation’s living standards and the billions paid to Ukraine’s defence.

This week Merz faced down opposition MPs in the Bundestag, the most vociferous from the pro-Kremlin AfD, who called for funding to Ukraine to be halted, as parliament debated the budget for 2027, Germany’s largest ever, due to be voted on by the weekend.

Opposition, however, is not only coming from the right. In Saxony-Anhalt, where in December the AfD may take over a state premiership for the first time, the BSW, a small, Russia-friendly, leftwing party, last month teamed up with the AfD to also demand a halt to arms supplies to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.

And on Thursday, an influential former Protestant church leader, pacifist and theologian, Margot Käßmann, called for a “change of course” and more diplomacy from the government.

“We must do everything we can to prevent war,” Käßmann said in an interview with DLF, a public broadcaster, insisting she would not bend to demands for Germans to defend themselves, instead calling for “much more diplomatic commitment”. She also accused Merz of not taking the “discomfort of the population seriously”.

Notably, the Körber survey found that the lowest support for Ukraine, 31%, was recorded in Germany’s eastern states, where the AfD – nationally five points ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance in the polls – has an increasing hold on power. Only 11% of east Germans are in favour of military help to Ukraine, while 75% would like to see a “normalisation” of relations with Russia, the survey found.

Merz now faces an uphill battle to win the German people round to his own government’s conviction that support for Ukraine is vital if Germany is to ensure its own security and future.

articles.title: Iran warns on Gulf military presence as South Korea readies expanded naval role
articles.summary: Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.
articles.preview: Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict. SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman.
articles.body:
Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.

SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke by telephone on Thursday (Nov 26) with South Korea's Cho Hyun, who reaffirmed Seoul did not intend to join any war or deploy troops to the Gulf, the Iranian embassy in Seoul said in an X post on Friday.

South Korea's parliament is reviewing a government motion to broaden the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to include the outer waters of the Gulf of Oman to help ensure safe navigation of its commercial vessels.

The anti-piracy Cheonghae unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009.

Araqchi said the presence of foreign militaries "would instead heighten tensions and expand the scope of conflict", the Iranian embassy said.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry said Cho explained that the mission of the navy unit was to ensure the safety of South Koreans and protect the country's economic interests.

South Korea, which is one of the world's largest oil and gas importers, sourced 70 per cent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, with most shipments delivered through the Strait of Hormuz, according to government data.

articles.title: A Gaza anche l’ambiente è sotto attacco
articles.summary: Più del 99 per cento di Gaza è contaminato da residui tossici, che avvelenano l’acqua, il terreno e l’aria
articles.preview: Mentre gli abitanti della Striscia di Gaza fanno i conti con il freddo e la pioggia, un altro pericolo incombe su di loro per i prossimi decenni. Metalli pesanti, residui di esplosivi, amianto proveniente dagli edifici distrutti, diossine e contaminanti biologici hanno trasformato il territorio in una “landa desolata e tossica”. Lo denuncia un rapporto pubblicato il 23 novembre dall’ong britannica Oxfam insieme al Conflict and environment observatory, che documenta le conseguenze ambientali e umanitarie dei conflitti armati e delle attività militari.
articles.body:
Mentre gli abitanti della Striscia di Gaza fanno i conti con il freddo e la pioggia, un altro pericolo incombe su di loro per i prossimi decenni. Metalli pesanti, residui di esplosivi, amianto proveniente dagli edifici distrutti, diossine e contaminanti biologici hanno trasformato il territorio in una “landa desolata e tossica”.

Lo denuncia un rapporto pubblicato il 23 novembre dall’ong britannica Oxfam insieme al Conflict and environment observatory, che documenta le conseguenze ambientali e umanitarie dei conflitti armati e delle attività militari.

Usando immagini satellitari, rilevamenti a distanza, analisi spaziali e altri dati open source, la ricerca ha concluso che più del 99 per cento della Striscia di Gaza presenta segni di contaminazione ambientale causata dagli attacchi israeliani degli ultimi tre anni. I residui tossici avvelenano l’acqua, contaminano il suolo e inquinano l’aria, mettendo ulteriormente a rischio le vite dei palestinesi.

Il direttore esecutivo di Oxfam international, Amitabh Behar, spiega nella presentazione del rapporto: “Il genocidio che Israele sta commettendo a Gaza comprende attacchi militari contro l’ambiente, che costituiscono crimini di guerra ambientali e minacciano la vita ora e per generazioni a venire”.

Con tutti e sei gli impianti di trattamento delle acque reflue fuori servizio, ogni giorno 40mila metri cubi di scarichi non trattati finiscono nelle falde acquifere e nel mar Mediterraneo. Le tempeste delle ultime settimanehanno aggravato la situazione perché la pioggia si è mischiata alle acque reflue riversandosi nelle strade e allagando le tende degli sfollati.

Queste acque contaminate poi penetrano nel sottosuolo, rendendo l’esposizione ai residui tossici continua e inevitabile. L’autrice del rapporto Lama Abdul Samad, esperta di questioni legate all’acqua e ai servizi igienico-sanitari, ha detto alla Bbc che a Gaza rischiano di aumentare le malattie respiratorie, i tumori, i danni agli organi, le malformazioni congenite e i casi di bambini nati morti.

L’anno scorso il Programma delle Nazioni Unite per l’ambiente ha calcolato che le operazioni militari israeliane hanno generato più di 61 milioni di tonnellate di detriti in tutta la Striscia di Gaza, il 15 per cento delle quali è potenzialmente a rischio elevato di contaminazione da sostanze pericolose.

Secondo Abdul Samad gestire i danni ambientali nel territorio sarà “estremamente impegnativo, perché la contaminazione è diffusa” e gli ordigni inesplosi impediscono “l’accesso alla maggior parte delle aree”.

Oxfam stima che per rimuovere queste montagne di macerie servirebbero 2,1 milioni di carichi di autocarri con cassone ribaltabile, pari a 736 giri intorno alla circonferenza del pianeta. La quantità di macerie da rimuovere è circa otto volte superiore a quella provocata dal conflitto del 2017 a Mosul, in Iraq.

Il precedente legale sul genocidio

Il rapporto di Oxfam sottolinea che la distruzione ambientale documentata a Gaza potrebbe rientrare nell’ambito di applicazione di diverse disposizioni dello statuto di Roma, che ha istituito la Corte penale internazionale, e della convenzione del 1948 per la prevenzione e la repressione del crimine di genocidio.

La distruzione ambientale non è di per sé un reato punibile in base allo statuto di Roma, chiarisce il rapporto. Tuttavia, prosegue, “la distruzione ambientale mirata o su larga scala può costituire, agevolare o fornire prove schiaccianti di crimini di guerra, crimini contro l’umanità e genocidio, qualora privi i civili delle condizioni necessarie alla sopravvivenza, causi gravi danni o sia usata nell’ambito di un attacco più ampio contro una popolazione civile”.

Sono tutti elementi che potrebbero avere un peso nella decisione della Corte internazionale di giustizia (Cig, il principale organo giudiziario delle Nazioni Unite) chiamata dal Sudafrica a stabilire se Israele sta commettendo un genocidio a Gaza.

L’argomento è tornato nel dibattito internazionale dopo che il 19 novembre la Cig ha emesso quella che Amnesty international ha definito una “sentenza storica” stabilendo che la Birmania (rinominata Myanmar dalla giunta militare) ha commesso un genocidio ai danni della minoranza musulmana dei rohingya durante le operazioni condotte dall’esercito nel 2016 e nel 2017.

Molti esperti sottolineano che la sentenza della Cig rafforzerà la causa per genocidio contro Israele, fissando un precedente secondo cui l’intento genocida può coesistere con un obiettivo militare.

Come scrive Anthony Samrani, condirettore di L’Orient-Le Jour, “il fatto che la Corte internazionale di giustizia abbia accertato il genocidio nel caso birmano non significa necessariamente che farà altrettanto nel procedimento che riguarda Israele. Ma se avesse escluso il genocidio nel caso birmano, sarebbe stato difficile giungere a una conclusione diversa per Gaza. E le ragioni per cui l’ha riconosciuto indeboliscono molto la linea difensiva israeliana”.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Mediorientale.

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

articles.title: 'Proof it happened': Photographers reflect on Duterte's drug war
articles.summary: Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
articles.preview: Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019. MANILA: Noel Celis's pulse still races whenever a motorcyclist pulls up alongside him at a red light, a legacy of countless nights photographing Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody drug war.
articles.body:
Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

MANILA: Noel Celis's pulse still races whenever a motorcyclist pulls up alongside him at a red light, a legacy of countless nights photographing Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody drug war.

"They call it riding in tandem," the freelance photographer told AFP of the two-man teams that once roamed the capital, Manila, dealing out death, conceding it remained "scary" after years of death threats tied to his work.

Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

For photographers like Celis, it is as if that period happened yesterday.

The 43-year-old, who worked for AFP at the time, photographed about 200 drug war killings.

One picture showed a young woman cradling the bloody body of her boyfriend shortly after he was gunned down at a busy intersection.

To the mainly Catholic nation, it bore a disturbing resemblance to Michelangelo's La Pieta, a sculpture of the Virgin Mary cradling Christ after his crucifixion. It swiftly became the defining image of the crackdown.

Those working the drug war beat took to calling themselves "nightcrawlers", after a Hollywood film about Los Angeles camera crews chasing late-night mayhem.

MENTAL MAP OF DEATH

At first, the journalists said, the police had no qualms about tipping them off about the killings.

But they clammed up as the public outcry grew, and the photographers resorted to chasing after mortuary vans summoned by police to collect the dead.

It all came flooding back for Dondi Tawatao, 46, when he returned with AFP to a garbage-strewn street where, on a rainy night 10 years ago, he took pictures of two bodies beneath the exposed roots of a banyan tree.

Near them were two handguns he believed were planted there.

"It was very dark, very sinister. It's supposed to be the tree of life, but on that night, it became the tree of death," he told AFP.

After shooting the drug war for four years, the killings became "normalised" to the point where he stopped visiting crime scenes unless they involved at least three corpses.

The long nights rearranged how he saw Manila, he said.

"You sort of have a mental map of where the killings took place. Like randomly, you would be walking, then you realise, 'this was where so-and-so was killed'."

He later left the profession, "primarily to take a rest mentally".

"WE WANT TO APOLOGISE"

Freelancer Kimberly dela Cruz, 36, found her first victim on Manila's rail tracks, and another atop a major bridge.

"It was a full moon, and I thought, 'What a beautiful evening it would have been - except somebody died'," she told AFP of the first.

The head of the man at the second scene was wrapped in packaging tape. He lay next to a cardboard poster that read: "I'm a drug pusher, don't emulate me."

Some of her colleagues would require professional counselling. One suffered from recurring nightmares about the drug war dead coming back to life.

Celis's memories centre on the heart-wrenching keening of victims' wives and mothers, and the sharp, metallic smell of blood.

Residents of the mainly slum-area killing grounds could fear journalists as much as they did police, dela Cruz said.

"I was an outsider. They thought I was an (intelligence operative), police, or somebody that would bring evil," she said.

Celis said photographers wrestled with feelings of guilt over not being able to help, and accusations of "profiting from the suffering of other people".

When he and a colleague attended the wake of the La Pieta victim, they half-dreaded a lynching by angry relatives.

"We went there to apologise for not being able to help," he said, telling the victim's girlfriend the pictures could be evidence were charges ever brought.

"I WAS SHOCKED"

"A picture is powerful," Celis said, "especially at this time, when standing history on its head is in vogue".

Alluding to Holocaust deniers, Tawatao said the photos provided "incontrovertible proof that it happened".

None of the photographers interviewed by AFP believed the drug war solved the country's narcotics problem.

They remain convinced the police murdered thousands to enforce Duterte's will.

But for all, Duterte's arrest and handover to the ICC last year seemed an impossibility - until it happened.

"I was shocked, because I didn't think it was possible. We've only seen the powers that be get away with it," Tawatao said.

Dela Cruz described a "huge sense of relief when (Duterte) was flown to The Hague. It meant some sort of justice was achieved by the families".

"He ordered a war on drugs that killed many people," Celis said.

"It's the natural consequence of his actions."

La élite del campo la cuestiona y la tacha de operación de márketing La historia se repite, pero esta vez no cuela, según algunos de los mayores expertos en una de las materias más complicadas —y trascendentales— que existen.
articles.body:
Ven Chandrasekaran, de Stanford, propone una descripción de la gravedad cuántica, difundida y aplaudida por Sam Altman en redes. La élite del campo la cuestiona y la tacha de operación de márketing

La historia se repite, pero esta vez no cuela, según algunos de los mayores expertos en una de las materias más complicadas —y trascendentales— que existen. El joven físico teórico Venkatesa Chandrasekaran acaba de publicar una posible descripción de la gravedad cuántica, uno de los mayores problemas de la física actual, que lleva más de un siglo sin poder resolverse. En su propuesta, aún no revisada por expertos independientes, le da las gracias tanto a OpenAI como a Sam Altman, el director ejecutivo de la compañía. Las formas y el fondo del anuncio son una muestra más del poder de los gigantes de la inteligencia artificial, no solo para atacar problemas que se pensaban irresolubles por mentes humanas, sino para hacerse publicidad con ellos, aunque eso suponga ignorar prácticas básicas del método científico, como la declaración de conflictos de interés.

Altman ha alabado el trabajo de Chandrasekaran. “Ven fue uno de los primeros creyentes en que podríamos usar nuestro modelo del momento para resolver los problemas del milenio”, ha escrito el ejecutivo en la red X. La gravedad cuántica no es uno de esos siete problemas matemáticos, pero está relacionada con varios de ellos, y según a quién se pregunte, es una presa mucho más complicada.

Ven was one of the earliest believers that we could use our then-current model to solve millenium prize problems.

There are a lot of brilliant people in the world, but being brilliant and also having correctly-placed confidence and courage to keep pushing on something that… https://t.co/ryBs1OX2gy

— Sam Altman (@sama) November 26, 2026

Las grandes compañías de IA compiten en la carrera por ver quién resuelve antes los mayores problemas de la ciencia: el último, esta misma semana, con la aparente solución del gigante de la IA Anthropic a la hipótesis de Riemann. En este contexto, aparece este preprint (un estudio no revisado por colegas) y Altman alaba la capacidad de este físico de seguir intentando algo que casi todo el mundo creía imposible. “Doy las gracias por tener tanta gente así en OpenAI”, ha añadido el magnate. Greg Brockman, presidente y cofundador de la empresa, también ha alabado el trabajo: “Hacia un conocimiento más profundo del universo”, ha escrito en X.

Parece publicidad, y según algunos popes de la física teórica, lo es. Aunque Chandrasekaran firma su propuesta como científico de Stanford únicamente, también ha formado parte del equipo de razonamiento de la empresa que dirige Altman.

El problema en cuestión es conectar la teoría general de la relatividad de Einstein, que describe la gravedad en el universo, con la física que opera en el mundo cuántico, donde las partículas elementales que componen los átomos tienen comportamientos totalmente imposibles, como estar en dos sitios a la vez. Son como dos mundos incompatibles y nadie por ahora ha conseguido explicar cómo opera la gravedad a escala cuántica.

Chandrasekaran dice haber alcanzado su solución trabajando en colaboración con el modelo GPT-6 Astra de la compañía OpenAI durante meses. El investigador agradece expresamente a la empresa por los 400 millones de tokens, unidades básicas de datos, que ha podido emplear para completar su trabajo.

Como ha sucedido con la hipótesis de Riemann o las ecuaciones de Navier-Stokes, los razonamientos de los científicos ayudados por la IA son tan complejos que ni siquiera los mayores expertos en la materia pueden seguirlos o entenderlos por sí mismos. En matemáticas existe un programa informático de verificación, llamado Lean, que permite determinar si la solución es válida o no.

Pero en física, el razonamiento matemático es solo parte de la solución, y no existe un equivalente informático que pueda validar o rechazar una propuesta, lo que complica mucho más saber si es solo una posibilidad más entre miles, o una contribución histórica que lo cambia todo. Todos los expertos consultados por este diario, y otros que han expresado sus opiniones espontáneamente debido a la polvareda levantada por la propuesta, creen que por ahora no se ha resuelto el problema de la gravedad cuántica.

Alejandro Vilar, físico teórico de la Universidad de la Columbia Británica, en Canadá, es tajante: “Estamos muy lejos de que esto sea una solución sólida a la gravedad cuántica”. “Es una propuesta interesante, pero hay dudas fundamentales sobre su validez”, añade.

El investigador traza otra línea clara entre matemáticas y física que, por ahora, se mantiene. “La capacidad de cálculo de la IA es impresionante, pero todos los que trabajamos en este campo no hemos visto aún que la IA sea capaz de conseguir un cambio conceptual del que sí han sido capaces grandes físicos en las últimas décadas. Eso sí, puede que en dos meses ya lo haya conseguido”, reconoce. El investigador también cuestiona las formas en las que llega esta propuesta. “Chandrasekaran trabaja en OpenAI, y hubiera sido más limpio que lo hubiera dicho abiertamente”. Vilar no cuestiona la valía del investigador, que es respetado por la comunidad, pero advierte que ha recibido más atención gracias a quiénes le han promocionado. “Un resultado de estas características es una oportunidad publicitaria muy grande para la inteligencia artificial y en particular para OpenAI”.

José Luis Barbón, del Instituto de Física Teórica (CSIC-UAM), cerca de Madrid, destaca la brillante carrera de Chandrasekaran. Hizo la tesis en Berkeley, estuvo después en el Instituto de Estudios Avanzados, donde también trabajó Einstein, y allí elaboró junto a otros físicos las versiones preliminares de su propuesta actual. “Al parecer esto es un proyecto personal suyo, que no usaría los modelos internos de frontera, sino los comerciales, pero con un montón de tokens de computación que le habrán dado por ser de la casa. Es lo que algunos llamarían un dragon rider [un jinete del dragón de la IA], o un teórico-ciborg, aumentado con IA. Parecido a Levent Alpöge, el que está detrás de la solución de Riemann de Anthropic, aunque ese parece que cabalga dragones prototipo tipo Fórmula 1, no dragones comerciales”, añade.

“Este paper sería interesante si fuera correcto, pero puede haber hipótesis técnicas que cambian la física y que no son aceptables; por eso hará falta mucho más escrutinio”, opina el científico. El punto más polémico es que parece capaz de calcular la cantidad de información que hay en el interior de un agujero negro a la longitud de Planck, la escala más pequeña conocida, y que es un billón de trillones más pequeña que un centímetro.

Jonathan Oppenheim, físico del University College, cree que la propuesta no llega “ni de lejos” a establecer una teoría de la gravedad cuántica. El investigador tacha el trabajo de “afirmación falsa” en un extenso análisis en su web. Como no hay nada equiparable a Lean en física, lamenta, “seguiremos recibiendo falsas alarmas como esta si no encontramos otras formas de distinguir la señal del ruido”. El investigador hace un llamamiento a la comunidad científica para que cree nuevas herramientas que permitan descartar rápido las propuestas inservibles. Oppenheim ha usado un enjambre de agentes de Anthropic para desbancar el artículo de Chandrasekaran identificando varias inconsistencias. “El próximo artículo quizá sea más difícil de desenmascarar que este. Antes de que aparezca, sería útil que nosotros, como comunidad, estableciéramos algunos criterios o pruebas que cualquier propuesta candidata tuviera que superar, como las tres comprobaciones mencionadas anteriormente”.

articles.title: Japan releases new guidelines on use of AI by Self-Defense Forces
articles.summary: The new guidelines build on the Defense Ministry's basic policy for promoting the use of artificial intelligence, released in 2024.
articles.preview: The Defense Ministry on Friday released new guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence by the Self-Defense Forces, setting out five basic principles, including one stipulating that humans retain decision-making authority and responsibility. In its Defense AI Vision, the ministry said it would move beyond individual applications of AI to a stage where the technology transforms how defense capabilities are exercised. The new guidelines build on the ministry’s basic policy for promoting the use of AI, released in 2024.
articles.body:
The Defense Ministry on Friday released new guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence by the Self-Defense Forces, setting out five basic principles, including one stipulating that humans retain decision-making authority and responsibility.

In its Defense AI Vision, the ministry said it would move beyond individual applications of AI to a stage where the technology transforms how defense capabilities are exercised.

The new guidelines build on the ministry’s basic policy for promoting the use of AI, released in 2024.

The ministry set out a policy of leveraging AI and data to strengthen defense capabilities.

The four other basic principles are: compliance with international and domestic laws; the assurance of safety, reliability, transparency and accountability; avoiding excessive reliance on specific technologies, products or businesses; and starting AI use with operational needs and challenges.

Regarding compliance with international and domestic laws, the guidelines said the ministry has no intention of developing fully autonomous lethal weapons that operate beyond human control.

The guidelines call for more efficient information processing through AI-based analysis of radar tracks, satellite and aerial imagery and signals intelligence, as well as the use of physical AI to conduct missions without putting personnel at risk.

On cooperation with allies and like-minded countries, the guidelines state that the ministry will seek to establish an environment in which information and analysis obtained from different systems and AI can be mutually understood and used in joint missions, while maintaining independent command and control structures as well as control over sensitive data.

articles.title: AI unleashes a new era of cybersecurity
articles.summary: A shortage of cybersecurity professionals remains one of the biggest barriers to resilience.
articles.preview: While there have been concerns about the safety and security of cyberspace since it was invented, the last few months have been especially harrowing. There have been high-profile hacks, outages and incidents that hammered home the vulnerabilities that come when societies are threaded together with virtual strings. Industry experts reckon that the total losses generated by cyberattacks in any given year is in the trillions of dollars; the figure is likely unknowable given the frequency and opacity of many if not most such incidents.
articles.body:
While there have been concerns about the safety and security of cyberspace since it was invented, the last few months have been especially harrowing. There have been high-profile hacks, outages and incidents that hammered home the vulnerabilities that come when societies are threaded together with virtual strings.

Industry experts reckon that the total losses generated by cyberattacks in any given year is in the trillions of dollars; the figure is likely unknowable given the frequency and opacity of many if not most such incidents. The headlines of the last few weeks suggest that we have entered an AI-empowered era in which the scale, scope, speed and frequency of those assaults will be significantly increased.

There is hope, however. The anxiety and recognition that AI creates a fundamentally new era for cybersecurity is the start. If governments, businesses and individuals adopt this new mindset, the damage will be mitigated, though we must be ready for steady-state anxiety.
